questions.question: The design receives 4 billion queries per day and plans for a 3x peak-to-average multiplier. What peak query rate should it model?
options: About 15,400 queries/s
About 46,300 queries/s
About 139,000 queries/s
About 4,000,000 queries/s
questions.explanation: Four billion divided by 86,400 is about 46,300 queries/s on average. Multiplying by three gives about 139,000 queries/s at peak.

questions.question: Why does the baseline use document sharding for the inverted index?
options: Every query can be answered by exactly one shard regardless of its terms.
Each shard can retrieve a local top-K independently, and the broker can merge the shard results.
Document sharding removes the need for a term dictionary and posting lists.
It guarantees that result quality is unchanged when most shards time out.
questions.explanation: A document shard owns the complete term index for its document subset, so it can produce local candidates independently. The cost is query fan-out and a global merge.

questions.question: What prevents query servers from reading a mixture of incompatible index segments and ranking features?
options: Write every posting update directly into all serving replicas.
Keep the newest segment on each server even if its feature version differs.
Pin each request to an atomically published manifest generation with compatible versions.
Use the result cache as the authoritative index version.
questions.explanation: The manifest is the publication boundary. It names a validated set of compatible segments, deletion state, metadata, and feature versions that a request pins consistently.

questions.question: Why combine small delta segments with periodic base-index compaction?
options: Delta segments improve freshness, while compaction bounds segment count and serving overhead.
Delta segments make deletion and versioning unnecessary.
Compaction lets the crawler ignore host politeness rules.
The combination removes all query-time shard fan-out.
questions.explanation: Frequent delta publication makes accepted changes visible quickly. Background compaction combines segments so query serving does not accumulate unbounded seeks and duplicate work.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes robots.txt in this design?
options: It is an authorization system that makes listed paths private.
It is a crawler coordination protocol; sensitive content still requires real access control.
It guarantees that every allowed URL will be indexed.
It is used only after a document has entered the serving index.
questions.explanation: RFC 9309 defines crawler access rules and handling. The protocol is not authentication, does not make paths secret, and does not guarantee indexing.

questions.question: A keyword-stuffed malware page receives a high lexical score. What should the ranking pipeline do?
options: Increase its authority weight until the final score becomes negative.
Serve it only when a whole-result cache contains the page.
Remove it through the hard eligibility policy regardless of its soft ranking score.
Wait for click-through rate to determine whether it is harmful.
questions.explanation: Eligibility is a correctness boundary, not another ranking weight. Ineligible content must be removed even when retrieval or freshness signals are strong.

questions.question: One document-shard group misses the query deadline. Which degraded response is most defensible?
options: Retry without a deadline until every shard responds.
Bypass current policy checks so the partial result returns faster.
Return measured partial results only above a coverage threshold, record the missing group, and avoid caching low-coverage output.
Publish a new index generation during the user request.
questions.explanation: A bounded deadline protects tail latency. Partial results are acceptable only under an explicit coverage policy, with observable missing shards and unchanged eligibility enforcement.

questions.question: Which evaluation plan best supports a ranking release?
options: Promote whenever aggregate click-through rate rises in a one-hour test.
Use graded relevance judgments and slice metrics offline, then shadow, canary, and run a predeclared online experiment with guardrails.
Measure only average latency because relevance is subjective.
Train and evaluate on the same clicked results without preserving exposure data.
questions.explanation: A reliable release combines judged offline quality, system and policy slices, production-like replay, shadow traffic, canary evidence, and a controlled online experiment. Clicks alone are biased by prior exposure and position.
